summary: The note describes the szlachta, the formalized hereditary noble class of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, covering its legal status, religion, size relative to the population, and the political privileges it gained. It traces key milestones such as the 1355 privilege of Casimir III, the 1492 free election, the 1505 Nihil novi act, and the liberum veto. It also covers the class's loss of privileges after the Partitions of Poland and the 1921 March Constitution, and the relationship between Polish and Lithuanian nobility.
one_line: The szlachta was the hereditary noble class of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, with privileges that grew from the 14th century until the partitions and 1921.
key_facts: The Polish term szlachta designated the formalized, hereditary noble class of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
In official Latin documents, hereditary szlachta are referred to as "nobilitas".
The first free election of a king in Poland took place in 1492, won by John I Albert.
On 3 May 1505, King Alexander I Jagiellon granted the Act "Nihil novi nisi commune consensu", which forbade the king to pass new laws without the consent of the nobility's representatives.
Between 1652 and 1791, any nobleman could nullify the proceedings of a sejm or sejmik by exercising the liberum veto, except in the case of a confederated sejm or sejmik.
In 1355 in Buda, King Casimir III the Great issued the first country-wide privilege for the nobility.
The szlachta's sovereignty ended in 1795 with the Partitions of Poland.
The legal privileges of the szlachta were legally abolished in the Second Polish Republic by the March Constitution of 1921.
The note states that the szlachta comprised around 8% of the total population in 1791, up from 6.6% in the 16th century.
Nobility in other European countries, except Spain, amounted to a mere 1–3% of the population, according to the note.
After the Counter-Reformation, the nobility became almost exclusively Catholic.
In the 18th century, many followers of Jacob Frank joined the ranks of Jewish-descended Polish gentry.
Despite having a king, Poland was called the nobility's Commonwealth because the king was elected by the hereditary nobility and the country was considered the property of this class.
In 1413, the existing Lithuanian nobility formally joined the szlachta class after a series of tentative personal unions.
Traditionally, szlachta members were owners of landed property, often in the form of manor farms called folwarks.
